title: IV. The Third Son, Alyosha
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: He was only twenty. His brother Ivan was in his twenty-fourth year at the time, and their eldest brother Dmitri was twenty-seven. First I must explain that this young man, Alyosha, was no fanatic and, in my opinion at least, not even a mystic. I may as well state my whole opinion at the outset. He was simply a lover of humanity from early on. He took up the monastic life only because, at that time, it struck him as the ideal way out for his soul, which was struggling up from the darkness of worldly wickedness toward the light of love. It struck him that way because he believed he had found in the monastery an extraordinary being, our celebrated elder, Zossima, and he had attached himself to Zossima with all the warm first love of his ardent heart. I don’t deny that he was very strange even then, and had been since the cradle. I have mentioned already that he lost his mother in his fourth year, yet remembered her all his life—her face, her caresses, “as though she stood living before me.” Such memories can reach back, as everyone knows, even to the age of two. But they seldom last a whole lifetime as isolated spots of light in the darkness, like the one corner left of a huge picture that has faded and vanished everywhere else. That is how it was with him. He remembered a still summer evening and an open window, with the slanting rays of the setting sun (that he recalled most vividly of all). In a corner of the room was the holy image with a lighted lamp before it, and on her knees in front of the image was his mother, sobbing hysterically, crying and moaning. She snatched him up in both arms and squeezed him so tight it hurt, and prayed for him to the Mother of God, holding him out in both arms toward the image as if to place him under the Mother’s protection ... and suddenly a nurse runs in and snatches him away from her in terror. That was the picture! And Alyosha remembered his mother’s face at that moment. He used to say it was frenzied but beautiful, as he remembered it. He rarely wanted to speak of this memory to anyone, though. As a child and a youth he was far from outgoing, and he talked very little. That was not from shyness or a sullen dislike of company. It was from something else, a kind of inner preoccupation, wholly his own and having nothing to do with other people, yet so important to him that it made him seem to forget them. But he was fond of people. All his life he seemed to trust people completely, and still no one ever thought him a simpleton or naïve. Something about him made you feel at once (and this held true all his life) that he had no wish to sit in judgment on others—that he would never presume to criticize, and would never condemn anyone for anything. He seemed, in fact, to accept everything without the least condemnation, although he often grieved bitterly. So thoroughly was this so, that even in his earliest youth nothing could surprise or frighten him. At twenty he came to his father’s house, a perfect sink of filthy debauchery. Chaste and pure as he was, he simply withdrew in silence whenever the sight became unbearable, and he showed no sign of contempt or condemnation. His father had once lived as a dependent himself, so he was touchy and quick to take offense, and he received Alyosha at first with distrust and sullenness. “He doesn’t say much,” he would say, “and he thinks the more.” But soon—within two weeks, in fact—he was embracing and kissing Alyosha terribly often, with drunken tears and sottish sentimentality. Still, he plainly felt a real and deep affection for him, the like of which he had never been capable of feeling for anyone before.

Everyone, in fact, loved this young man wherever he went, and that had been so since his earliest childhood. When he entered the household of his patron and benefactor, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, he won the hearts of the whole family, who came to look on him quite as their own child. Yet he went to live there at such a tender age that he could not have been calculating or scheming to win affection. The gift of making himself loved immediately and unconsciously was simply inborn in him, part of his nature, so to speak. It was the same at school, though he seemed exactly the sort of child that other children distrust, sometimes ridicule, and even dislike. He was dreamy, for example, and rather solitary. From his earliest years he loved to creep into a corner and read, and yet he was a general favorite all the time he was at school. He was seldom playful or merry, but you could see at a glance that this was not sullenness. On the contrary, he was cheerful and good-tempered. He never tried to show off among his schoolmates. Perhaps for that reason, he was afraid of no one, yet the boys realized at once that he took no pride in his fearlessness and seemed not to know he was bold and brave. He never resented an insult. An hour after being wronged, he might speak to the one who had done it, or answer his question, with a look as trusting and open as if nothing had passed between them. It was not that he seemed to have forgotten the insult, or made up his mind to forgive it. He simply did not count it as an insult, and this completely won over the boys and captivated them. He had one trait that made all his schoolmates, from the lowest class to the highest, want to mock him—not out of malice, but because it amused them. That trait was a wild, fanatical modesty and chastity. He could not stand to hear certain words and certain talk about women. Unhappily, there are “certain” words and talk that no one can stamp out in schools. Boys who are pure in mind and heart, hardly more than children, love to discuss among themselves, and even out loud, things and pictures and images that even soldiers would think twice about mentioning. More than that, much that soldiers know nothing of is familiar to quite small children of our educated and upper classes. It isn’t moral depravity, or any real inner corruption and cynicism, but it has the look of those, and among the boys it is often considered refined, subtle, daring, and worth copying. When they saw Alyosha Karamazov stick his fingers in his ears whenever they talked of “that,” they would sometimes crowd around him, pull his hands away, and shout filth into both his ears. He would struggle, slip down onto the floor, and try to hide, without saying one word of abuse, and endure their insults in silence. In the end, though, they left him alone and stopped teasing him as a “regular girl.” What’s more, they came to view it with pity, as a weakness. In class he was always among the best, but never first.

When Yefim Petrovitch died, Alyosha had two more years to go at the provincial gymnasium. The inconsolable widow left almost at once for a long stay in Italy, taking her whole family, which consisted only of women and girls. Alyosha moved into the house of two distant relations of Yefim Petrovitch, ladies he had never met. He did not know himself on what terms he lived with them. It was very typical of him, in fact, never to care whose money was paying for him. In this he was a striking contrast to his elder brother Ivan, who fought poverty through his first two years at the university, kept himself by his own efforts, and had felt bitterly, from childhood on, that he lived at his benefactor’s expense. But I don’t think we should judge this odd trait of Alyosha’s too harshly. Anyone who knew him even slightly would have seen that Alyosha was one of those young men, almost the religious-enthusiast type, who would give away a sudden large fortune to the first person who asked, whether for good works or perhaps to some clever rogue. In general he hardly seemed to know the value of money—not in the literal sense, of course. When he was given pocket money, which he never asked for, he was either terribly careless with it and spent it in a moment, or he held on to it for weeks, not knowing what to do with it.
In later years Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, a man very sensitive about money and middle-class honesty, passed the following judgment on Alyosha, once he had got to know him:

“Here is perhaps the one man in the world you could leave alone without a penny, in the middle of an unknown city of a million people, and he would come to no harm. He wouldn’t die of cold or hunger, since someone would feed and shelter him at once. And if no one did, he would find shelter himself, and it would cost him no effort or humiliation. Sheltering him would be no burden to anyone; it would more likely be seen as a pleasure.”

He did not finish his studies at the gymnasium. With a year of the course still to go, he suddenly told the ladies that he was off to see his father about a plan that had come into his head. They were sorry, and did not want to let him go. The trip was not an expensive one, but the ladies would not let him pawn his watch, a parting gift from his benefactor’s family. They gave him plenty of money, and even fitted him out with new clothes and linen. He gave half of the money back, though, saying he intended to go third class. When he reached town, he did not answer his father’s first question, why he had come before finishing school, and he seemed, so they say, unusually thoughtful. Soon it became clear that he was looking for his mother’s tomb. He more or less admitted at the time that this was the only reason for his visit. Still, it can hardly have been the whole reason. More likely he did not understand himself, and could not have said, what had suddenly stirred in his soul and drawn him irresistibly down a new road, unknown but unavoidable. Fyodor Pavlovitch could not show him where his second wife was buried. He had never visited her grave since the day he threw earth on her coffin, and over the years he had forgotten altogether where she lay.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, by the way, had been away from our town for some time before this. Three or four years after his wife died, he went off to the south of Russia and eventually turned up in Odessa, where he spent several years. At first, as he put it, he got to know “a lot of low Jews, Jewesses, and Jewkins,” and he ended up being welcomed by “Jews high and low alike.” We may suppose that it was in this period that he developed a peculiar knack for making money and hoarding it. He came back to our town for good only three years before Alyosha arrived. His old acquaintances found him terribly aged, though he was by no means an old man. He carried himself not exactly with more dignity, but with more effrontery. The old buffoon now had an insolent itch to turn other people into buffoons. His depravity with women was not merely what it had been, but even more revolting. In a short time he opened a great number of new taverns in the district. It was plain that he had perhaps a hundred thousand roubles, or not much less. Many people in the town and the district were soon in his debt, and had put up good security, naturally. Lately, too, he looked somehow bloated. He seemed more irresponsible and more erratic, and had sunk into a sort of incoherence: he would start one thing and go on with another, as though he were letting himself go altogether. He got drunk more and more often. And without that same servant Grigory, who by then had aged a good deal himself, and who sometimes looked after him almost like a tutor, Fyodor Pavlovitch might have landed in terrible scrapes. Alyosha’s arrival seemed to touch even his moral side, as though something that had long been dead in his soul had woken up in this prematurely old man.

“Do you know,” he often said, looking at Alyosha, “you’re like her, ‘the crazy woman’”—that was what he called his dead wife, Alyosha’s mother. It was Grigory who showed Alyosha the “crazy woman’s” grave. He took him to our town cemetery and pointed out, in a remote corner, a cast-iron tombstone, cheap but decently kept. It bore the name and age of the dead woman and the date of her death, with a four-line verse underneath, the sort commonly seen on old-fashioned middle-class graves. To Alyosha’s amazement, the tomb turned out to be Grigory’s doing. He had put it up over the poor “crazy woman’s” grave at his own expense, after Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom he had often pestered about the grave, left for Odessa and abandoned both the grave and all his memories. Alyosha showed no particular emotion at the sight of his mother’s grave. He just listened to Grigory’s detailed and solemn account of how the tomb was built, stood there with his head bowed, and walked away without a word. It was perhaps a year before he went to the cemetery again. But this little episode had an effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch—and a very original one. He suddenly took a thousand roubles to our monastery to pay for requiems for his wife’s soul. Not for the second wife, Alyosha’s mother, the “crazy woman,” though, but for the first, Adelaïda Ivanovna, the one who used to thrash him. That same evening he got drunk and ran down the monks to Alyosha. He was far from religious himself; he had probably never set so much as a penny candle in front of a saint’s image. Strange surges of sudden feeling and sudden thought are common in men of that type.

I have already said that he looked bloated. His face by now carried unmistakable marks of the life he had led. There were long fleshy bags under his small eyes, which were always insolent, suspicious, and ironical, and a mass of deep wrinkles in his little fat face. His Adam’s apple hung below his sharp chin like a great fleshy goiter, which gave him a peculiar, repulsive, sensual look. On top of that came a long, rapacious mouth with full lips, and between them you could see little stumps of black, rotten teeth. He slobbered whenever he began to speak. He enjoyed making jokes about his own face, though I believe he was quite pleased with it. He liked above all to point to his nose, which was not very large, but very fine and noticeably hooked. “A regular Roman nose,” he would say, “and with my goiter I look just like an ancient Roman patrician of the decadent period.” He seemed proud of it.

Soon after visiting his mother’s grave, Alyosha suddenly announced that he wanted to enter the monastery, and that the monks were ready to accept him as a novice. He explained that he wanted this very much, and that he was solemnly asking for his father’s consent. The old man knew that the elder Zossima, who lived in the monastery’s hermitage, had made a special impression on his “gentle boy.”

“Well, he’s the most honest monk of the lot, of course,” he remarked, after listening to Alyosha in thoughtful silence, and seeming hardly surprised at the request. “H’m!... So that’s where you want to be, my gentle boy?”

He was half drunk, and suddenly he broke into his slow, half-drunken grin, which had a bit of cunning and tipsy slyness in it. “H’m!... I had a feeling you’d end up in something like this. Would you believe it? You were making straight for it. Well, of course you have your own two thousand. That’s a dowry for you. And I’ll never desert you, my angel. I’ll pay whatever they need for you there, if they ask. But if they don’t ask, why should we bother them? What do you say? You know, you spend money like a canary, two grains a week. H’m!... Do you know that near one monastery there’s a place outside the town where every baby knows that nobody lives but ‘the monks’ wives,’ as they’re called? Thirty women, I believe. I’ve been there myself. You know, it’s interesting in its own way, of course, as a change. The trouble is, it’s awfully Russian. No French women there. Of course they could get them fast enough, they’ve got plenty of money. If word gets out, they’ll turn up. Well, here there’s nothing of the sort, no ‘monks’ wives,’ and two hundred monks. They’re honest. They keep the fasts. I’ll admit it.... H’m.... So you want to be a monk? And do you know, I’m sorry to lose you, Alyosha; would you believe it, I’ve really got fond of you? Well, it’s a good chance. You’ll pray for us sinners; we’ve sinned too much here. I’ve always wondered who would pray for me, and whether there’s anyone in the world who would. My dear boy, I’m awfully stupid about that. You wouldn’t believe it. Awfully. You see, stupid as I am about it, I keep thinking, I keep thinking—now and then, of course, not all the time. I can’t imagine, I think, that the devils would forget to drag me down to hell with their hooks when I die. Then I wonder—hooks? Where would they get them? What from? Iron hooks? Where do they forge them? Have they got some sort of foundry down there? The monks in the monastery probably believe there’s a ceiling in hell, for instance. Now, I’m ready to believe in hell, but without a ceiling. That makes it more refined, more enlightened, more Lutheran, that is. And after all, what difference does it make whether it has a ceiling or not? But there’s a damnable question hidden in it, you know? If there’s no ceiling, there can be no hooks, and if there are no hooks, the whole thing collapses, which is unlikely too, because then nobody would drag me down to hell, and if they don’t drag me down, where’s the justice in the world? _Il faudrait les inventer_, those hooks, on purpose for me alone, because if you only knew, Alyosha, what a blackguard I am.”
“But there are no hooks there,” Alyosha said, looking at his father gently and seriously.

“Yes, yes, only the shadows of hooks, I know, I know. That’s how a Frenchman described hell: ‘_J’ai vu l’ombre d’un cocher qui avec l’ombre d’une brosse frottait l’ombre d’une carrosse._’ How do you know there are no hooks, darling? Once you’ve lived with the monks, you’ll change your tune. But go and find out the truth there, and then come and tell me. Anyway, it’s easier to go to the other world if you know what’s there. Besides, it’ll be more fitting for you with the monks than here with me, a drunken old man, and young harlots ... though you’re like an angel, nothing touches you. I expect nothing will touch you there either. That’s why I’m letting you go, because I hope so. You’ve got all your wits about you. You’ll burn, and you’ll burn out; you’ll be healed and come back again. And I’ll wait for you. I feel you’re the only creature in the world who hasn’t condemned me. My dear boy, I feel it, you know. I can’t help feeling it.”
And he actually started blubbering. He was sentimental. He was wicked and sentimental.
